explanations.answer: The day He was taken up to heaven
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. The writer says the first book covers all that Jesus began to do and to teach, "…until the day He was taken up to heaven…" (Acts 1:2). So the book runs right up to that exact day. Quite the stretch for one book.

explanations.answer: The day He was born in Bethlehem
explanations.explanation: Birth day is a fair guess, friend, but the writer doesn't stop there. He says the first book goes "…until the day He was taken up to heaven…" (Acts 1:2). That's much further down the road. Nobody wraps up a book on the first page, not even me.

explanations.answer: The day He was baptized by John
explanations.explanation: John does show up in this passage, so I see the pull. Jesus mentions that "…John baptized with water…" (Acts 1:5). But the writer says the first book goes "…until the day He was taken up to heaven…" (Acts 1:2). That day is the one the book runs to.

Yes, friend. Jesus gave instructions through the Holy Spirit to "…the apostles He had chosen." (Acts 1:2). Chosen is the key word there. He picked them Himself, and I think that's worth sitting with for a second.

Elders are real people in the Bible, baker, but they're not the ones here. The verse says Jesus gave His instructions to "…the apostles He had chosen." (Acts 1:2). Elders aren't in this verse at all. Only the apostles are.

Scribes are in the Bible, friend, so I get why the word came to mind. But this verse says Jesus gave instructions to "…the apostles He had chosen." (Acts 1:2). Scribes aren't mentioned in this verse. Only the apostles are.

True, baker! After His suffering, Jesus presented Himself to them "…with many convincing proofs that He was alive." (Acts 1:3). Many proofs, not just one. I think if I'd seen that, I'd have needed to sit down and fan myself with a cookie sheet.

This one is actually true, friend. The text says that after His suffering, Jesus "…presented Himself to them with many convincing proofs that He was alive." (Acts 1:3). Many, not a few. He appeared to them over a span of forty days.

That's it, friend. Jesus says, "Do not leave Jerusalem, but wait for the gift the Father promised, which you have heard Me discuss." (Acts 1:4). They'd already heard Him talk about it. Now the job was to stay put and wait.

The Roman governor never comes up here, baker. Jesus tells them to wait for "…the gift the Father promised…" (Acts 1:4). It's a gift from the Father, not an order from any government office. Different kind of mail entirely.

explanations.answer: A message from the high priest
explanations.explanation: No high priest in this passage, friend. Jesus says to wait for "…the gift the Father promised, which you have heard Me discuss." (Acts 1:4). That gift comes from the Father, and they'd already heard Jesus talk about it.

Not quite, baker. Jesus says, "…in a few days you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit." (Acts 1:5). A few days is not many years. I'd never leave a batch in the oven for years, and Jesus isn't leaving them waiting that long either.
False is right, friend. Jesus says, "…in a few days you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit." (Acts 1:5). Just a few days. That's why He tells them to stay in Jerusalem and wait.

explanations.answer: Will You restore the kingdom to Israel now
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. They ask, "Lord, will You at this time restore the kingdom to Israel?" (Acts 1:6). The passage says earlier that Jesus spoke about the kingdom of God (Acts 1:3). I respect a baker who just asks.

explanations.answer: Who will lead us once You are gone
explanations.explanation: Good question, friend, but it's not the one they ask. They say, "Lord, will You at this time restore the kingdom to Israel?" (Acts 1:6). Their question is about the kingdom and the timing. Nothing in the verse about who leads.

explanations.answer: Will You take us with You to heaven
explanations.explanation: Not this time, baker. What they ask is, "Lord, will You at this time restore the kingdom to Israel?" (Acts 1:6). It's all about the kingdom and when. They don't ask to go along.

Close, but no, friend. Jesus says, "It is not for you to know times or seasons that the Father has fixed by His own authority." (Acts 1:7). So the times belong to the Father. I think that's a relief, honestly, because I'd peek at the oven timer every five seconds.

That's right, baker. Jesus says, "It is not for you to know times or seasons that the Father has fixed by His own authority." (Acts 1:7). The Father fixed them, and they're not the apostles' to know. I think that's a relief, honestly.
Yes, baker! Jesus says, "…you will be My witnesses…" (Acts 1:8). A witness tells what they've seen and heard. That's a big job, and they were handed it straight from Jesus.
I see why rulers came to mind, since they'd just asked about a kingdom. But Jesus says, "…you will be My witnesses…" (Acts 1:8). He gives them a different job. A witness tells what they know.
Guards is a fun guess, friend, but not what Jesus says. He tells them, "…you will be My witnesses…" (Acts 1:8). Standing watch isn't the job He names. He calls them witnesses.

explanations.answer: To the ends of the earth
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Jesus says they'll be His witnesses "…in Jerusalem, and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth." (Acts 1:8). It starts with Jerusalem and goes all the way out. That's a long list, and the last item is HUGE.

Syria is a real place in the Bible, but it's not on His list. Jesus says, "…in Jerusalem, and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth." (Acts 1:8). He goes far bigger than one region, friend.

Egypt is all over the Bible, baker, but Jesus doesn't name it here. He says they'll be witnesses "…in Jerusalem, and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth." (Acts 1:8). The ends of the earth. That covers a whole lot more than one land.

Yep, a cloud. The verse says, "…they watched as He was taken up, and a cloud hid Him from their sight." (Acts 1:9). They watched the whole thing until the cloud covered Him. Nothing fancy added, baker.

A whirlwind carried Elijah, the prophet, up in 2 Kings 2:11, so I see where that came from. But here the verse says, "…a cloud hid Him from their sight." (Acts 1:9). Different story, different ride, friend.
A bright light is a fair guess, baker, but it's not in this verse. The text says, "…a cloud hid Him from their sight." (Acts 1:9). So they watched Him go up, and then a cloud covered Him.

True, baker! The verse says they "…were looking intently into the sky as He was going, when suddenly two men dressed in white stood beside them." (Acts 1:10). Suddenly is the word. One second it's just them and the sky, and the next there are two more.

This one is true, friend. While they were looking intently into the sky, "…suddenly two men dressed in white stood beside them." (Acts 1:10). The text says suddenly. I think that would have made me drop a whole tray.

explanations.answer: He will come back the same way He went
explanations.explanation: You've got it, baker. The two men say, "This same Jesus, who has been taken from you into heaven, will come back in the same way you have seen Him go into heaven." (Acts 1:11). That's why my ovens stay ready. As for when, Jesus says no one knows the day or the hour except the Father (Matthew 24:36).

explanations.answer: They will not see Him again on earth
explanations.explanation: Not what they said, friend. The two men say, "This same Jesus, who has been taken from you into heaven, will come back in the same way you have seen Him go into heaven." (Acts 1:11). They tell the apostles He will come back. That's the word they give.

explanations.answer: They should go look for Him in Galilee
explanations.explanation: Galilee is where the men get the name from, baker. They call the apostles "Men of Galilee…" (Acts 1:11). But they never send them off to look there. They say this same Jesus "…will come back in the same way you have seen Him go into heaven." (Acts 1:11).
